Um, I met Ed Catmull, um, who was the, who was running the computer division of Lucas film, uh, in 1985.
And Ed showed me what they were doing, uh, and he shared with me his dream about making the first computer animated feature film.
And I bought into that dream both financially and spiritually.
And it, it took us 10 years to do that, uh, but we did it.
And, uh, the first computer animated feature film, first totally computer synthetic film of any kind, which was Toy Story.
Fortunately, uh, um, it came out really well.
And it became the third most successful animated film of any type, um, in terms of box office success.

So, um, the things that that captured me were I've I've been involved in graphics most of my life.
Um, the Apple 2, most people don't remember was the first real color computer that you could get your hands on, cheap, cheap one.
Um, the Macintosh, obviously was graphics, the laser writer was graphics, but it was all 2D.
And, and we'd done some 3D work at Apple and I was certainly aware of the field and and the stuff that Ed and his team were doing was way ahead of anything I'd ever seen anyone do.
Uh, and I think Pixar still holds that mantle today.
You know, I think it's the Mecca of high-end computer graphics.

Yeah, well Pixar is a studio.
Um, I'm not a filmmaker.
Uh, I don't direct our films.
John Lasseter does and I think he's the most brilliant director working in animation today.
Uh, what I try to do is help create the environment where all these incredible people can make films.
So, we've got a whole creative team, which is about 100 people now.
And we've got an incredible technical team, and we got an incredible production team, and we figured out a way to have all those people work together as peers.
Um, that's a really unique thing in the industry in that, um, you know, the the very best creative people will only go to work at a few places.
Disney, Pixar, um, possibly Dreamworks.
Um, but the very best people, it's it's it's very hard for these other places to get them.
In the same, uh, in the same sense, the very best computer scientists in computer graphics will only go to work at a few places.
And Pixar is one of those.
But most of the studios are not because they don't have that level of a technical culture there.
And I think Pixar is the only place in the world that can hire the best from both of these areas.
And we've worked for 10 years to, to figure out a way to have them all work together, which is not easy because they come from very the Hollywood culture and the Silicon Valley culture are really different.
And, um, you know, we think we've picked the best from both.
So.

Well, Sillywood's a term for a lot of, you know, Sillywood is a, a term that was invented for the space that a lot of companies were in so they could raise investment, but they never produced any products.
You know, it was sort of technology meeting Hollywood.
And, uh, Pixar is the only, only company I know where Silicon Valley and Hollywood have met where there's actually been any offspring that have been successful.

I learn a lot.

It's the same thing.

How do we do that?

They take that into the editing room and they build their film.
And hopefully they can do a good job because if they can't, it's too late.
The actors are gone, the sets are down.

And therefore the only conclusion you can come to is you have to edit your film before you make it.

Every single day we worry about how can we make Pixar a better company so that nobody will ever want to leave.
And we don't take anybody for granted.
Um, because if they don't want to be at Pixar, then then probably they should leave anyway, uh, whether or not they would ever have a contract.
So, you know, we've watched Silicon Valley, which is, you know, four or five times as big as Hollywood, uh, has grown up much faster than Hollywood, uh, and has grown up on this different model and we think it's a pretty good model, so we adopted it.
And so far it's working really well.

Uh, I don't know.
I mean, I don't think about this all the time.
Um, you know, one of the differences that I've noticed between content and, uh, technology, selling technology boxes is that, you know, you can hardly find, I mean, I'll relate it to my own life.

Disney released its first animated feature film, Snow White in 1937, that's 60 years ago.

I don't I don't think I know one person who doesn't, who hasn't seen it.

I mean, these are our myths.
And here's something that's 60 years old that's regenerating itself in my son and other young children.
And, you know, I think people are going to be watching Toy Story in 60 years.
Um, not because of the computer graphics, but because of the story, you know, about friendship.
And that's something really amazing to me.
Something very different than than the industry I worked in in the past.
And to have the opportunity to put these stories into the culture like this, if we can, if we can work really hard and be lucky, uh, again and again, uh, is a rare opportunity.
And I think everybody at Pixar feels really, really privileged to, to have this opportunity.
So that's that's what we're all about and we want to, we want to make these products that hopefully will be around for a long time and everybody will get a lot of, you know, enjoyment from and learn from.

Oh, that, obviously, you know, yeah.
